docs.d: SQL is a declarative language for defining and querying relational data. What the standard covers, and why every engine still differs.
docs.h: what is sql? sql is a declarative language for defining and querying relational data. what the standard covers, and why every engine still differs. sql definition ansi standard declarative query language history sql (structured query language) is a **declarative** language for defining, manipulating and querying data held in a relational database. you describe *what* result you want; the database's query planner decides *how* to produce it — which indexes to use, which join algorithm to run, in what order. that single property explains most of sql's character. there is no loop in `select`, no explicit "open file, scan rows". the same query can execute in 3 milliseconds or 3 minutes depending on statistics, indexes and data volume, without a character of it changing. a worked example select d.name as department, count(*) as headcount, round(avg(e.salary)) as avg_salary from employees e join departments d on d.id = e.department_id where e.hired_at >= date '2020-01-01' group by d.name having count(*) > 5 order by avg_salary desc; nowhere does that statement say "scan the employees table, hash the departments table, aggregate into a hash map". it states a relationship and a shape. the engine picks the strategy. the standard, and what it is worth sql is standardised by iso/iec 9075. the revisions that matter in practice: | revision | year | notable additions | | --- | --- | --- | | sql-92 | 1992 | the baseline most people mean by "standard sql": `join` syntax, subqueries, `case`, string/date types | | sql:1999 | 1999 | recursive queries (`with recursive`), triggers, user-defined types, `grouping sets` | | sql:2003 | 2003 | window functions, `merge`, sequence generators, xml | | sql:2008 | 2008 | `fetch first … rows only`, `instead of` triggers, `truncate` | | sql:2011 | 2011 | temporal tables (system- and application-time periods), extended window frames | | sql:2016 | 2016 | `json` functions, row pattern matching (`match_recognize`), polymorphic table functions | | sql:2023 | 2023 | `json` data type, property graph queries (sql/pgq), `any_value` | ::: warn conformance is partial, everywhere no shipping database implements the full standard, and every database ships features the standard never described. treat "standard sql" as a *portability budget*, not a guarantee. this reference marks each construct as ansi or vendor-specific, and shows the differences rather than averaging them away. ::: the sublanguages sql is usually split into functional groups. the boundaries are conventional, not defined by the standard, but the vocabulary is universal: | group | stands for | statements | | --- | --- | --- | | **ddl** | data definition language | `create`, `alter`, `drop`, `truncate`, `comment` | | **dml** | data manipulation language | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `merge` | | **dcl** | data control language | `grant`, `revoke` | | **tcl** | transaction control language | `begin`, `commit`, `rollback`, `savepoint` | some texts classify `select` separately as dql (data query language). nothing depends on the label. logical evaluation order sql clauses are *written* in one order and *evaluated* in another. this is the single most useful thing a beginner can memorise, because it explains three quarters of "why can't i use my alias there?" errors. 1. from — resolve tables, apply joins 2. where — filter individual rows 3. group by — collapse rows into groups 4. having — filter groups 5. select — evaluate expressions, assign aliases 6. distinct — remove duplicate result rows 7. order by — sort the result 8. limit/offset— slice the result so a `select` alias is not visible in `where` (step 2 runs before step 5) but *is* visible in `order by` (step 7 runs after): select price * quantity as line_total from order_items where price * quantity > 100 -- must repeat the expression, alias not yet assigned order by line_total desc; -- alias is fine here ::: note engines that relax this mysql, mariadb, sqlite and clickhouse permit `select` aliases in `group by` and `having`; mysql also allows them in `having` per the standard. bigquery, snowflake and databricks additionally allow aliases in `where` in many positions. postgresql, sql server and oracle do not — code written against the permissive engines does not port. ::: set semantics, not row semantics a sql table is a **multiset** (a bag): unordered, duplicates allowed unless a constraint forbids them. two consequences trip people up constantly: **there is no default order.** without `order by`, a result's row order is undefined and may change between runs, after a vacuum, or when the plan changes to a parallel scan. **`null` is not a value.** it is a marker for "unknown", and it makes comparisons three-valued. see [null handling](/sql/null/). tables, rows, columns :: /sql/relational-model/ :: the data model underneath the language null and three-valued logic :: /sql/null/ :: why null = null is not true select :: /sql/select/ :: the statement you will write most dialect comparison :: /comparison/ :: the same task in eight dialects

docs.h: relational databases, tables, rows & columns relations, tuples and attributes — and what tables, rows and columns actually guarantee in a real engine. relational model table row column tuple attribute relation cardinality degree normalization the relational model, defined by e. f. codd in 1970, represents all data as **relations**: unordered sets of tuples over a set of named, typed attributes. sql implements this model loosely — it uses multisets rather than sets, and it adds `null` — but the vocabulary maps directly. | relational theory | sql | meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | relation | table | a named collection of rows with a fixed column list | | tuple | row / record | one entity instance | | attribute | column / field | one named, typed property | | domain | data type | the permitted set of values | | cardinality | row count | how many rows | | degree | column count | how many columns | tables a table has a name, an ordered column list, and zero or more rows. column *order* is part of the table definition (it affects `select *` and `insert` without a column list) but is otherwise not meaningful — always name your columns explicitly in production code. create table employees ( id bigint primary key, -- identity email varchar(255) not null unique, -- natural key, enforced full_name varchar(120) not null, department_id int references departments(id), salary numeric(12,2) check (salary >= 0), hired_at date not null default current_date, manager_id bigint references employees(id) -- self-reference ); ::: tip name things in the singular or plural, but pick one there is no technical difference. `employees` (plural table, singular row) is the most common convention in application schemas; oracle shops often use singular. consistency matters far more than the choice. ::: rows a row is one instance. two rows are *duplicates* if every column compares equal — which, thanks to `null`, is subtler than it sounds: two rows both containing `null` in a column are treated as duplicates by `distinct`, `group by` and `union` (which use "not distinct from" semantics), but `null = null` in a `where` clause is unknown, not true. select distinct department_id from employees; -- one row for all the nulls select * from employees where department_id = null; -- always zero rows select * from employees where department_id is null; -- correct columns every column carries a **name**, a **data type**, an optional **default**, a **nullability** flag and optional **constraints**. types are not decoration — they determine storage size, comparison and sort behaviour, index compatibility and overflow rules. | property | set by | notes | | --- | --- | --- | | type | `column_name type` | see the [data types explorer](/datatypes/) | | nullability | `not null` | columns are nullable by default | | default | `default expr` | applied when the column is omitted from `insert`, not when `null` is passed explicitly | | collation | `collate` | governs comparison and sort order for text | | generated | `generated always as (…)` | computed from other columns; stored or virtual | | identity | `generated … as identity` | auto-numbering; see [sequences](/sql/sequences/) | normalization, in one screen normalization removes redundancy so that each fact is stored exactly once. the forms in practical use: **1nf** — every column holds a single atomic value; no repeating groups, no comma-separated lists in a text column. **2nf** — 1nf, plus every non-key column depends on the *whole* primary key (only relevant with composite keys). **3nf** — 2nf, plus no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies). **bcnf** — a stricter 3nf: every determinant is a candidate key. ::: note the practical rule design in 3nf, then denormalize deliberately, with measurements, when a read path demands it. analytical warehouses (redshift, snowflake, bigquery, databricks) routinely use wide denormalized star schemas because joins across billions of rows cost more than duplicated columns. ::: -- not 1nf: a list in a column. cannot be indexed or joined usefully. create table orders_bad (id int, product_names text); -- 'widget, gizmo, doodad' -- 1nf+: one row per fact, joinable, indexable, constrainable. create table orders (id int primary key, customer_id int not null); create table order_items ( order_id int not null references orders(id), product_id int not null references products(id), quantity int not null check (quantity > 0), primary key (order_id, product_id) ); physical storage differs sharply by engine the logical model is shared; the physical layout is not, and it drives performance advice that does not transfer between engines. | engine | row layout | consequence | | --- | --- | --- | | postgresql | heap + separate indexes | index scans need a heap fetch unless the index covers the query (index-only scan) | | mysql/innodb | clustered by primary key | secondary indexes store the pk, so lookups cost two traversals; keep the pk narrow | | sql server | heap or clustered index | the clustered index *is* the table | | sqlite | b-tree per table, rowid-keyed | `without rowid` tables cluster on the declared pk | | redshift / snowflake / bigquery / clickhouse | columnar blocks | reading fewer *columns* is what saves i/o; `select *` is genuinely expensive |

docs.h: primary keys & foreign keys surrogate vs natural keys, composite keys, referential actions, and the engine-specific behaviour of auto-increment. primary key foreign key composite surrogate natural identity autoincrement serial referential integrity cascade primary keys a primary key uniquely identifies each row. it implies `not null` + `unique`, and every mainstream engine backs it with an index automatically. -- column constraint create table users (id bigint primary key, email text not null); -- table constraint (required for composite keys) create table order_items ( order_id int not null, product_id int not null, quantity int not null, constraint pk_order_items primary key (order_id, product_id) ); -- added later alter table users add constraint pk_users primary key (id); surrogate vs natural keys | | surrogate (generated id) | natural (real-world value) | | --- | --- | --- | | stability | never changes | changes when the world changes (email, isbn, vat number) | | width | narrow — 4/8 bytes | often wide text, inflating every secondary index | | joins | fast integer comparison | slower string comparison, collation-sensitive | | meaning | none — needs a lookup to interpret | self-describing | | recommendation | default choice for oltp | add as a `unique` constraint alongside the surrogate | ::: tip the usual answer use a surrogate primary key **and** a `unique` constraint on the natural key. you get stable joins plus enforced business uniqueness. do not rely on the surrogate alone — without the `unique` constraint nothing stops two rows with the same email. ::: auto-generated keys, per engine this is one of the least portable areas of sql. create table t (id int generated always as identity primary key, name text); create table u (id int generated by default as identity primary key, name text); -- preferred (pg 10+): standard identity create table t (id bigint generated always as identity primary key); -- legacy but still ubiquitous: serial types create a sequence + default create table t (id bigserial primary key); create table t (id bigint unsigned not null auto_increment primary key); select last_insert_id(); create table t (id bigint identity(1,1) primary key); select scope_identity(); -- sql server 2012+ also supports sequences and standard identity -- integer primary key aliases the internal rowid; the autoincrement keyword -- only prevents id reuse and adds overhead — usually omit it. create table t (id integer primary key, name text); -- 12c+ create table t (id number generated always as identity primary key); -- pre-12c pattern create sequence t_seq; create table t (id number primary key); -- then: insert into t values (t_seq.nextval); ::: warn warehouses do not enforce keys redshift, snowflake, bigquery, databricks and synapse accept `primary key`/`foreign key` declarations but **do not enforce them**. they exist purely as optimizer hints. duplicate rows will land silently; deduplicate in your pipeline. redshift and snowflake will produce wrong results from a query the optimizer rewrote assuming an unenforced uniqueness constraint you violated. ::: foreign keys a foreign key requires that each non-`null` value in the referencing column exists in the referenced column, which must be a primary key or unique constraint. create table orders ( id bigint primary key, customer_id bigint not null, constraint fk_orders_customer foreign key (customer_id) references customers (id) on delete restrict on update cascade ); referential actions | action | on delete of the parent | on update of the parent key | | --- | --- | --- | | `no action` | reject — check deferred to end of statement/transaction | reject | | `restrict` | reject immediately, cannot be deferred | reject immediately | | `cascade` | delete the children too | propagate the new value | | `set null` | set the child column to `null` (must be nullable) | same | | `set default` | set the child column to its default | same | ::: danger on delete cascade is a loaded gun a single `delete` on a parent can silently remove millions of descendant rows across a deep tree, inside one transaction, holding locks the whole time. it is right for genuinely owned data (order → order_items) and wrong for anything a human might want back. prefer `restrict` plus an explicit archival step for everything else. ::: postgresql=y mysql=y~innodb_only sqlite=w~pragma_foreign_keys=on sqlserver=y oracle=y~no_on_update db2=y cockroachdb=y mariadb=y redshift=n~declarative_only snowflake=n~declarative_only bigquery=n~declarative_only databricks=n~declarative_only clickhouse=n trino=n ::: warn two footguns worth memorising **sqlite** does not enforce foreign keys unless you run `pragma foreign_keys = on;` on **every connection** — the default is off for backwards compatibility. **oracle** has no `on update` clause at all. primary key values are expected to be immutable; propagate updates with a trigger or, better, don't update keys. ::: always index your foreign keys only postgresql, sql server and oracle leave the referencing column unindexed by default; mysql/innodb creates one automatically. an unindexed fk column makes every parent delete or update perform a full scan of the child table, and in oracle it escalates to a share lock on the whole child table. create index idx_orders_customer_id on orders (customer_id);

docs.d: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, EXCLUDE and deferrable constraints — with the enforcement gaps in each engine.
docs.h: constraints not null, unique, check, default, exclude and deferrable constraints — with the enforcement gaps in each engine. constraint not null unique check default exclude deferrable validate enforced constraints are declarative rules the database enforces on every write, from every client, forever. application-level validation is advisory; a constraint is the only thing that actually guarantees an invariant holds. the catalogue | constraint | guarantees | index created? | | --- | --- | --- | | `not null` | value is present | no | | `unique` | no two rows share the value | yes (all major engines) | | `primary key` | `unique` + `not null`, one per table | yes | | `foreign key` | value exists in the referenced table | not automatically (except mysql) | | `check` | a boolean expression holds per row | no | | `default` | supplies a value when the column is omitted | no | | `exclude` | no two rows satisfy a set of operator comparisons | yes (gist) — postgresql only | create table bookings ( id bigint generated always as identity primary key, room_id int not null references rooms(id), guest_email text not null, guests int not null default 1, period tstzrange not null, status text not null default 'pending', constraint ck_guests check (guests between 1 and 8), constraint ck_status check (status in ('pending','confirmed','cancelled')), constraint ck_email check (guest_email like '%@%'), constraint uq_ref unique (room_id, period), -- no two confirmed bookings for the same room may overlap in time: constraint ex_overlap exclude using gist (room_id with =, period with &&) where (status = 'confirmed') ); unique and null `unique` permits multiple `null`s in most engines, because two unknowns are not known to be equal. sql server is the notable exception. | engine | `null`s allowed in a unique column | | --- | --- | | postgresql | many. pg 15+ adds `unique nulls not distinct` to opt into single-null behaviour | | mysql / mariadb | many | | sqlite | many | | oracle | many (but a composite unique key with all columns null is not stored) | | **sql server** | **exactly one** — a second `null` violates the constraint | | db2 | one by default; `excluding null keys` on an index changes it | create unique index uq_one_active_session on sessions (user_id) where ended_at is null; create unique index uq_one_active_session on sessions (user_id) where ended_at is null; -- filtered index check constraints a `check` passes when the expression is `true` **or `unknown`**. a row with `null` in the checked column therefore passes unless you also declare `not null` — a subtle and common source of dirty data. create table products ( price numeric check (price > 0) -- null price is accepted! ); create table products_fixed ( price numeric not null check (price > 0) ); postgresql=y mysql=y~8.0.16+_enforced mariadb=y sqlite=y sqlserver=y oracle=y db2=y cockroachdb=y duckdb=y redshift=n snowflake=n~parsed_not_enforced bigquery=n databricks=w~constraint_on_delta trino=n clickhouse=w~constraint_on_insert ::: warn mysql before 8.0.16 parsed and ignored check mysql accepted `check` syntax from 5.x onward but silently did nothing with it until 8.0.16. if you inherit a schema from that era, the constraints you think you have may never have been enforced. re-validate the data before relying on them. ::: adding constraints to a live table validating an existing table takes a lock and a full scan. postgresql and oracle let you split the two phases. -- 1. add unvalidated: brief access exclusive lock, no scan. new rows are checked. alter table orders add constraint ck_total check (total >= 0) not valid; -- 2. validate later: share update exclusive only, does not block reads or writes. alter table orders validate constraint ck_total; alter table orders add constraint ck_total check (total >= 0) enable novalidate; alter table orders modify constraint ck_total validate; alter table orders with nocheck add constraint ck_total check (total >= 0); -- the constraint is now 'untrusted' and the optimizer will ignore it: alter table orders with check check constraint ck_total; -- makes it trusted again deferrable constraints a deferred constraint is checked at `commit` rather than at statement end — necessary for circular references and for bulk swaps of unique values. alter table pages add constraint uq_slot unique (slot) deferrable initially immediate; begin; set constraints uq_slot deferred; update pages set slot = 2 where id = 1; -- transiently duplicates slot 2 update pages set slot = 1 where id = 2; commit; -- checked here, and passes postgresql=y oracle=y db2=y cockroachdb=w~unique_only mysql=n~fks_deferred_only_in_a_sense sqlserver=n sqlite=w~fk_only_deferrable bigquery=n snowflake=n redshift=n ::: note sql server and mysql have no deferrable constraints in sql server, drop and recreate the constraint, or use a temporary sentinel value. in mysql, `set foreign_key_checks = 0` disables fk checking for the session — a blunt instrument that lets you commit inconsistent data, so re-enable it and validate afterwards. :::

docs.d: NULL is not a value. How three-valued logic changes comparisons, aggregates, joins, uniqueness and NOT IN.
docs.h: null & three-valued logic null is not a value. how three-valued logic changes comparisons, aggregates, joins, uniqueness and not in. null is null coalesce nvl ifnull nullif three valued logic unknown not in trap empty string `null` marks the **absence of a value** — "unknown" or "not applicable". it is not zero, not an empty string, and not equal to another `null`. every comparison involving it yields `unknown`, giving sql a three-valued logic. the truth tables true false unknown true true false unknown false false false false unknown unknown false unknown true false unknown true true true true false true false unknown unknown true unknown unknown `where` keeps a row only when the predicate is `true`. `unknown` is discarded exactly like `false` — which is why the following returns nothing at all: select * from employees where manager_id = null; -- 0 rows, always select * from employees where manager_id <> null; -- 0 rows, always select * from employees where manager_id is null; select * from employees where manager_id is not null; the not in trap this is the single most expensive `null` bug in production sql. if the subquery returns **even one** `null`, `not in` returns no rows. select * from employees where id not in (select manager_id from employees); the reason: `id not in (1, 2, null)` expands to `id <> 1 and id <> 2 and id <> null`, and that last term is `unknown`, so the whole conjunction can never be `true`. -- 1. not exists — correct, and usually the best plan (anti-join) select e.* from employees e where not exists (select 1 from employees m where m.manager_id = e.id); -- 2. filter the nulls out of the subquery select * from employees where id not in (select manager_id from employees where manager_id is not null); -- 3. left join … is null select e.* from employees e left join employees m on m.manager_id = e.id where m.id is null; ::: tip prefer not exists it is `null`-safe by construction, expresses the intent ("no matching row"), and postgresql, sql server and oracle all compile it to an anti-join. `not in` frequently blocks that optimization. ::: null in aggregates aggregate functions **ignore `null`** — except `count(*)`, which counts rows rather than values. select count(*) as all_rows, -- counts every row count(bonus) as rows_with_bonus, -- ignores null bonuses count(distinct dept) as distinct_depts, -- ignores null depts avg(bonus) as avg_bonus, -- sum(bonus)/count(bonus), not /count(*) sum(bonus) as total_bonus -- null if every bonus is null from employees; ::: warn avg is not what you may think `avg(bonus)` divides by the number of **non-null** bonuses. if you want nulls treated as zero, say so: `avg(coalesce(bonus, 0))`. the two produce different numbers on the same data, and both are "right" for different questions. ::: note also that `sum` over an empty or all-`null` set returns `null`, not `0`. wrap it if a number is required: `coalesce(sum(x), 0)`. the null-handling functions | function | behaviour | engines | | --- | --- | --- | | `coalesce(a, b, …)` | first non-null argument | ansi — universal | | `nullif(a, b)` | `null` when `a = b`, else `a` | ansi — universal | | `ifnull(a, b)` | two-argument coalesce | mysql, sqlite, bigquery, databricks | | `nvl(a, b)` | two-argument coalesce | oracle, redshift, db2 | | `nvl2(a, b, c)` | `b` if `a` is not null, else `c` | oracle, redshift | | `isnull(a, b)` | two-argument coalesce | sql server, synapse | | `a is not distinct from b` | null-safe equality | postgresql, db2, cockroachdb, duckdb, trino | | `a <=> b` | null-safe equality | mysql, mariadb, sqlite, databricks | select name, coalesce(nickname, first_name, 'anonymous') as display_name, revenue / nullif(orders, 0) as avg_order_value -- no divide-by-zero from customers; null-safe comparison select * from staging s join target t on t.id = s.id where s.email is distinct from t.email; -- true when one side is null and the other is not select * from staging s join target t on t.id = s.id where not (s.email <=> t.email); where (s.email <> t.email) or (s.email is null and t.email is not null) or (s.email is not null and t.email is null) sorting the standard leaves `null` ordering implementation-defined but provides `nulls first` / `nulls last`. | engine | default in `order by x asc` | `nulls first/last` supported | | --- | --- | --- | | postgresql, oracle | nulls **last** | yes | | mysql, mariadb, sqlite, sql server | nulls **first** | sqlite 3.30+ and mariadb yes; mysql and sql server no | | bigquery, snowflake, duckdb, databricks | nulls first (snowflake: last) | yes | select * from tasks order by case when due_date is null then 1 else 0 end, -- nulls last, everywhere due_date; ::: danger oracle: '' is null oracle treats the zero-length string as `null` for `varchar2`. `where name = ''` never matches, and `insert … values ('')` stores a `null`. this is oracle-specific and long-standing; no other major engine behaves this way. migrations to and from oracle must handle it explicitly. :::

docs.h: schemas, catalogs & naming three-part naming, search paths, and what "database" and "schema" mean in each engine — they are not the same thing. schema catalog database namespace search_path qualified name public dbo identifier quoting case sensitivity the standard defines a three-level namespace: **catalog → schema → object**. engines map their own concepts onto it inconsistently, which is why a "database" in mysql is a "schema" in postgresql. | engine | catalog | schema | cross-container query in one statement? | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | postgresql | database | schema (`public` default) | no — one database per connection (or use fdw / dblink) | | mysql / mariadb | *(unused)* | database == schema | **yes** — `db1.t` joined to `db2.t` | | sql server / synapse | database | schema (`dbo` default) | yes — `db.schema.table` | | oracle | database / pdb | user == schema | within a pdb; across pdbs via db links | | sqlite | attached db (`main`, `temp`) | *(none)* | yes, after `attach database` | | snowflake | database | schema | yes — `db.schema.table` | | bigquery | project | dataset | yes — `` `project.dataset.table` `` | | redshift | database | schema | yes (cross-database read via federated names) | | databricks | catalog | schema | yes — unity catalog `catalog.schema.table` | create schema analytics; create table analytics.daily_revenue (day date primary key, amount numeric(14,2)); select * from analytics.daily_revenue; drop schema analytics cascade; -- cascade drops contained objects too resolution: search_path and friends unqualified names are resolved against an ordered list of schemas. show search_path; -- "$user", public set search_path to analytics, public; -- session alter role reporting set search_path to analytics, public; -- per role alter database app set search_path to app, public; -- per database use analytics; -- mysql, sql server, snowflake, clickhouse alter session set current_schema = analytics; ::: danger search_path is a security boundary a function running as `security definer` with an attacker-controlled `search_path` can be tricked into calling a shadowed function or reading a shadowed table. always pin it: create function admin_op() returns void language plpgsql security definer set search_path = pg_catalog, public -- pinned as $$ … $$; ::: identifier quoting and case unquoted identifiers are **case-insensitive** but get folded to a canonical case — and the engines disagree on which case. | engine | unquoted folds to | quote character | quoted is case-sensitive | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | postgresql | lower | `"name"` | yes | | oracle, db2, snowflake | upper | `"name"` | yes | | sql server | preserved (comparison follows the collation) | `[name]` or `"name"` | depends on collation | | mysql / mariadb | preserved | backtick-quoted `name` or `"name"` in ansi_quotes mode | table names follow the filesystem; columns are case-insensitive | | sqlite | preserved, compared case-insensitively | `"name"`, `[name]`, backtick-quoted `name` | no | | bigquery | preserved; datasets/tables case-sensitive | backtick-quoted `project.dataset.table` | yes | create table "mytable" (id int); docs.h: views & materialized views stored queries, updatable views, with check option, and the refresh strategies for materialized views in each engine. view materialized view create view updatable check option refresh concurrently indexed view a **view** is a named query. it stores no data: every reference re-executes the underlying statement, and the optimizer usually inlines it into the calling query. create view active_customers as select c.id, c.email, c.created_at, sum(o.total) as lifetime_value from customers c join orders o on o.customer_id = c.id where c.status = 'active' group by c.id, c.email, c.created_at; select * from active_customers where lifetime_value > 1000; views are worth using for three reasons: they hide join complexity behind a stable name, they act as a **security boundary** (grant on the view, not the base tables), and they give you a compatibility layer when the physical schema has to change under a live application. ::: note views are not a performance feature a plain view costs the same as pasting its body into your query — no more, no less. if you need the result cached, you want a **materialized view** or a summary table. ::: updatable views the standard allows `insert`/`update`/`delete` through a view when the engine can map each result row unambiguously to exactly one base row: a single base table, no aggregation, no `distinct`, no `group by`, no set operations, no window functions. create view eu_customers as select id, email, country from customers where country in ('de','fr','es','it'); update eu_customers set email = 'x@y.z' where id = 42; -- writes through `with check option` stops writes that would create rows the view cannot see: create view eu_customers as select id, email, country from customers where country in ('de','fr') with check option; insert into eu_customers values (99, 'a@b.c', 'us'); -- error: new row violates check option for view "eu_customers" for anything more complex, intercept the write with a trigger: create function customers_view_insert() returns trigger language plpgsql as $$ begin insert into customers (email, country) values (new.email, new.country) returning id into new.id; return new; end $$; create trigger trg_insert instead of insert on customer_summary for each row execute function customers_view_insert(); postgresql=y mysql=y~simple_views_auto sqlite=w~instead_of_triggers_only sqlserver=y~instead_of oracle=y db2=y mariadb=y cockroachdb=w duckdb=n bigquery=n snowflake=n redshift=n materialized views a materialized view stores the **result**. queries read the stored rows; the trade-off is staleness plus refresh cost. create materialized view daily_revenue as select date_trunc('day', created_at) as day, sum(total) as revenue from orders group by 1 with data; -- a unique index is required for concurrently: create unique index on daily_revenue (day); refresh materialized view daily_revenue; -- takes an access exclusive lock refresh materialized view concurrently daily_revenue; -- readers keep working, slower create materialized view daily_revenue build immediate refresh fast on commit -- incremental, needs a materialized view log enable query rewrite -- optimizer can silently substitute it as select trunc(created_at) as day, sum(total) as revenue from orders group by trunc(created_at); create view dbo.daily_revenue with schemabinding as select cast(created_at as date) as day, sum(total) as revenue, count_big(*) as cnt from dbo.orders group by cast(created_at as date); create unique clustered index ix_daily_revenue on dbo.daily_revenue (day); -- from here the view is maintained on every write to dbo.orders create materialized view daily_revenue as select date_trunc('day', created_at) as day, sum(total) as revenue from orders group by 1; -- snowflake: single-table only, no joins, no order by; maintained by a background service. create materialized view daily_revenue_mv engine = summingmergetree order by day as select todate(created_at) as day, sum(total) as revenue from orders group by day; -- fires on insert into orders and writes the aggregate. it does not see pre-existing rows -- and does not see rows removed by delete. | engine | incremental refresh | auto refresh | query rewrite | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | postgresql | no — full rebuild | no (schedule it) | no | | oracle | yes (`fast`, with mv logs) | `on commit` / `on demand` | yes | | sql server (indexed view) | yes — synchronous | always | yes (enterprise) | | snowflake | yes — background service | yes | yes | | bigquery | yes — incremental | yes (`enable_refresh`) | yes | | redshift | yes (`auto refresh yes`) | yes | yes | | databricks | yes (delta live tables / mvs) | scheduled | limited | | clickhouse | insert-time only | on insert | no | | mysql / sqlite / duckdb | **not supported** — use a table + scheduled job | — | — | ::: warn "materialized view" means five different things in oracle and sql server it can be maintained transactionally; in postgresql it is a manual snapshot; in clickhouse it is an insert trigger that never sees historical rows. read the engine's page before assuming the semantics you know carry over. :::

docs.h: sequences & identity columns generating unique numbers: sequences, identity columns, caching, gaps, and why sequences are not transactional. sequence nextval currval identity autoincrement serial gaps cache cycle uuid snowflake id a **sequence** is a schema object that hands out numbers. an **identity column** is a column wired to an implicit sequence. both exist to generate surrogate keys without a race between concurrent inserts. create sequence order_id_seq start with 1000 increment by 1 minvalue 1000 maxvalue 9223372036854775807 cache 50 no cycle; insert into orders (id, total) values (next value for order_id_seq, 99.00); | operation | postgresql | oracle / db2 | sql server | mariadb | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | next value | `nextval('s')` | `s.nextval` | `next value for s` | `nextval(s)` | | last value (this session) | `currval('s')` | `s.currval` | — (`scope_identity()`) | `lastval(s)` | | reset | `setval('s', 1)` | `alter sequence … restart` | `alter sequence … restart with 1` | `alter sequence … restart` | ::: warn sequences are not transactional, by design `nextval` is exempt from rollback. if a transaction consumes id 42 and then rolls back, 42 is gone forever. **gaps are normal and unavoidable** — a sequence guarantees uniqueness and monotonicity, never contiguity. if you need gapless numbering (invoice numbers in many jurisdictions), you need a counter table plus a serialised update, and you must accept the write contention that comes with it. ::: begin; update invoice_counters set last_number = last_number + 1 where year = 2026 returning last_number into v_number; -- row lock held to commit insert into invoices (number, …) values (v_number, …); commit; identity columns create table orders ( id bigint generated always as identity primary key, -- cannot be overridden -- or: generated by default as identity -- may be supplied explicitly total numeric(12,2) ); `generated always` rejects an explicit value unless you override it, which is what you want in normal operation but painful during a data migration: insert into orders (id, total) overriding system value values (5, 10.00); -- then repair the sequence, or the next natural insert will collide: select setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('orders','id'), (select max(id) from orders)); set identity_insert dbo.orders on; insert into dbo.orders (id, total) values (5, 10.00); set identity_insert dbo.orders off; dbcc checkident ('dbo.orders', reseed); ::: danger the single most common migration bug loading rows with explicit ids and forgetting to advance the sequence. everything works until the first natural insert, which then fails with a duplicate key error — often days later, in production. reseed as the last step of every restore or bulk load. ::: cache and the cost of a crash `cache n` preallocates `n` values per session in memory. it removes a catalog write per insert (a large throughput win) at the cost of losing the unused block on crash or disconnect — bigger gaps. oracle's default cache is 20; postgresql's is 1. under heavy concurrent insert load in postgresql, raising the cache is a real optimization; in a cluster with logical replication, remember each node caches separately. distributed alternatives a central sequence is a coordination point that does not scale across nodes or regions. | strategy | sortable | coordination | notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `uuidv4` | no | none | random; terrible for clustered-index locality (page splits in innodb/sql server) | | `uuidv7` | yes (time-ordered) | none | now the default recommendation; pg 18 ships `uuidv7()`, others via extension | | ulid | yes | none | 26-char lexicographically sortable, same idea as uuidv7 | | snowflake id | yes | node id assignment | 64-bit: timestamp + node + counter; fits `bigint` | | `unique_rowid()` | roughly | none | cockroachdb built-in; avoids the hot-range problem of sequential keys | -- postgresql 18+ create table events (id uuid primary key default uuidv7(), payload jsonb); -- earlier versions: pg_uuidv7 extension, or generate in the application create table events (id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(), payload jsonb); ::: warn uuidv4 as a clustered primary key in mysql/innodb and sql server the primary key determines physical row order. random uuids scatter inserts across every page in the table, causing page splits, write amplification and a buffer pool that no longer fits the working set. use `uuidv7`/ulid, or store a `bigint` key and keep the uuid as a secondary unique column. :::

docs.h: alter changing live schemas: which alters are instant, which rewrite the table, and how to migrate without downtime. alter table add column drop column rename modify change lock ddl online migration zero downtime `alter table` is where portability and *safety* diverge most sharply. the same statement can be a metadata-only flick in one engine and a multi-hour full-table rewrite holding an exclusive lock in another. the operations alter table customers add column phone varchar(32); alter table customers drop column phone; alter table customers rename column full_name to display_name; alter table customers rename to clients; alter table customers add constraint ck_country check (length(country) = 2); alter table customers drop constraint ck_country; changing a column type is the least portable statement in common use: | engine | syntax | | --- | --- | | postgresql, db2, cockroachdb | `alter table t alter column c type bigint using c::bigint` | | mysql / mariadb | `alter table t modify c bigint not null` (repeat every attribute!) | | sql server / synapse | `alter table t alter column c bigint not null` | | oracle | `alter table t modify (c number(19))` | | sqlite | not supported — rebuild the table | | snowflake, bigquery | widening only (`int64`→`numeric`, `varchar(10)`→`varchar(20)`) | ::: danger mysql modify discards omitted attributes `alter table t modify c bigint` on a column that was `not null default 0 comment 'x'` silently drops the `not null`, the default and the comment. you must restate the entire column definition every time. ::: sqlite: the twelve-step rebuild sqlite supports only `add column`, `rename column`, `rename to` and `drop column` (3.35+). everything else means recreating the table. pragma foreign_keys = off; begin; create table customers_new ( id integer primary key, email text not null, country text not null default 'us' -- the change ); insert into customers_new (id, email, country) select id, email, 'us' from customers; drop table customers; alter table customers_new rename to customers; create index idx_customers_email on customers (email); -- recreate indexes/triggers commit; pragma foreign_key_check; pragma foreign_keys = on; what locks, and for how long this table is the difference between a deploy and an outage. | operation | postgresql | mysql 8 (innodb) | sql server | oracle | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `add column` (nullable, no default) | instant, metadata only | instant (`algorithm=instant`) | instant | instant | | `add column` with a constant default | instant (pg 11+) | instant (8.0.12+) | instant (2012+, enterprise) | instant (11g+) | | `add column` with a volatile default | full rewrite | rewrite | rewrite | rewrite | | `drop column` | instant (space reclaimed on rewrite) | rebuild (`inplace`, online) | instant metadata | `set unused` is instant | | `alter column type` (widening) | rewrite (some no-ops in 12+) | often rebuild | often instant | often instant | | `add index` | `create index concurrently` avoids blocking | `algorithm=inplace`, online | `with (online=on)` (enterprise) | `online` | | `add not null` | full scan; pg 12+ can use a matching `check` to skip it | rebuild | scan | scan (or `novalidate`) | create index concurrently idx_orders_customer on orders (customer_id); -- slower, cannot run inside a transaction, and can leave an invalid index -- if it fails — check with: select indexrelid::regclass from pg_index where not indisvalid; alter table orders add column note varchar(255), algorithm = instant; -- if mysql cannot do it instantly it errors instead of silently locking the table for an hour. alter table orders add index idx_note (note), algorithm = inplace, lock = none; ::: tip always set a lock timeout before ddl an `alter` waiting on a long-running query queues behind it — and every *subsequent* query queues behind the `alter`. a metadata-only change can take a healthy database down. bound the wait: set lock_timeout = '3s'; -- postgresql set lock_wait_timeout = 3; -- mysql (session) set lock_timeout 3000; -- sql server (ms) alter table orders add column note text; ::: the expand–contract migration the portable pattern for changing a column without downtime, on any engine: **expand** — add the new column (nullable, no default). instant. **dual-write** — deploy code writing both old and new. **backfill** — copy in batches (`where id between … `), committing each batch, with a pause between them. **verify** — count mismatches; add the `not null` constraint as `not valid`, then validate. **switch reads** — deploy code reading the new column. **contract** — stop writing the old column, then drop it in a later release. do $$ declare last_id bigint := 0; begin loop update orders set total_cents = (total * 100)::bigint where id > last_id and id <= last_id + 10000 and total_cents is null; exit when not found; last_id := last_id + 10000; commit; -- pg 11+ inside procedures; use a driver loop otherwise perform pg_sleep(0.05); -- let replication and autovacuum keep up end loop; end $$; ::: warn transactional ddl is not universal postgresql, sqlite, sql server, db2 and cockroachdb can roll back ddl inside a transaction — a failed migration leaves nothing behind. **mysql and oracle commit implicitly** before and after each ddl statement, so a multi-statement migration that fails halfway leaves the schema in a partial state. write mysql and oracle migrations to be individually idempotent. :::

-- what you meant double quotes make aliases with spaces or case; single quotes are **strings**, not identifiers (sql server and mysql accept them here, but it is not portable): select total as "total revenue" from orders; -- portable select distinct removes duplicate result rows after the select list is evaluated. it considers `null`s equal to each other. select distinct country, city from customers; -- distinct pairs, not distinct countries postgresql adds `distinct on`, which keeps the first row per group according to `order by`: select distinct on (customer_id) customer_id, id, total, created_at from orders order by customer_id, created_at desc; select count(*) from customers where country = 'de'; -- 1. verify the target set update customers set country = 'de' where country = 'de'; -- check the reported row count matches rollback; -- or commit update from another table every engine solves this differently — one of the sharpest dialect splits in sql. update orders o set customer_country = c.country from customers c where c.id = o.customer_id and o.customer_country is distinct from c.country; update o set o.customer_country = c.country from orders o join customers c on c.id = o.customer_id; update orders o join customers c on c.id = o.customer_id set o.customer_country = c.country; update orders o set customer_country = (select c.country from customers c where c.id = o.customer_id) where exists (select 1 from customers c where c.id = o.customer_id); ::: warn omitting the exists guard nulls out non-matching rows in the correlated form, rows with no matching customer get `null` — the subquery returns nothing. the `where exists` clause restricts the update to rows that actually have a match. this bug is easy to miss because it looks like it worked. ::: update orders set customer_country = c.country from customers c where c.id = orders.customer_id; update orders set status = 'archived' where status = 'closed' and closed_at < now() - interval 1 year order by id limit 5000; update top (5000) dbo.orders set status = 'archived' where status = 'closed' and closed_at < dateadd(year, -1, sysutcdatetime()); docs.h: merge / upsert the standard merge statement, its concurrency caveats, and the native upsert syntax in engines that lack it. merge upsert on conflict on duplicate key when matched slowly changing dimension scd2 idempotent load `merge` applies inserts, updates and deletes to a target table from a source in one statement — the standard way to express an upsert or a warehouse load. merge into customers as t using staging_customers as s on t.id = s.id when matched and s.is_deleted = true then delete when matched and (t.email, t.country) is distinct from (s.email, s.country) then update set email = s.email, country = s.country, updated_at = current_timestamp when not matched then insert (id, email, country) values (s.id, s.email, s.country); postgresql=y~15+ oracle=y sqlserver=y db2=y snowflake=y bigquery=y databricks=y synapse=y teradata=y~ redshift=y~2023+ duckdb=y~1.4+ mysql=n~on_duplicate_key sqlite=n~on_conflict clickhouse=n cockroachdb=n~upsert trino=y~connector_dependent when the engine has no merge insert into customers (id, email, country) select id, email, country from staging_customers on conflict (id) do update set email = excluded.email, country = excluded.country, updated_at = now() where (customers.email, customers.country) is distinct from (excluded.email, excluded.country); insert into customers (id, email, country) select id, email, country from staging_customers as s on duplicate key update email = s.email, country = s.country; upsert into customers (id, email, country) select id, email, country from staging_customers; ::: note on conflict needs a unique index `on conflict (col)` requires an actual unique constraint or unique index on `col` — the "conflict target". without one, postgresql raises *"there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the on conflict specification"*. use `on conflict on constraint constraint_name` to be explicit. ::: concurrency: merge is not atomic against concurrent writers under `read committed`, two concurrent `merge` statements can both find no matching row and both attempt an insert; one fails with a duplicate key error, or worse, both succeed if no unique constraint exists. **postgresql**: `insert … on conflict` *is* internally atomic and is the safe choice under concurrency. `merge` (15+) is not — it can raise a unique violation and must be retried. **sql server**: `merge` requires `holdlock`/`serializable` on the target to be safe: `merge into t with (holdlock)`. without it, deadlocks and duplicate-key errors under load are well documented. **oracle**: `merge` takes row locks as it goes; concurrent inserts of the same key still collide. a unique constraint plus retry is the reliable pattern. merge into dbo.customers with (holdlock) as t using (select @id as id, @email as email) as s on t.id = s.id when matched then update set email = s.email when not matched then insert (id, email) values (s.id, s.email); ::: warn always put a unique constraint behind an upsert whatever syntax you use, the only thing that actually prevents duplicates under concurrency is a unique index. the statement then either succeeds or raises a violation you can retry — instead of silently writing two rows. ::: a slowly changing dimension (type 2) merge into dim_customer as t using ( select s.customer_id, s.email, s.country, current_date as effective_from from staging_customer s ) as s on t.customer_id = s.customer_id and t.is_current = true when matched and (t.email <> s.email or t.country <> s.country) then update set t.is_current = false, t.effective_to = s.effective_from when not matched then insert (customer_id, email, country, effective_from, effective_to, is_current) values (s.customer_id, s.email, s.country, s.effective_from, date '9999-12-31', true); -- note: a single merge cannot both close the old row and insert the new one for the -- same key. run the insert of new versions as a second statement. ::: danger merge cannot match a target row twice if the source contains two rows with the same join key, standard `merge` raises an error ("attempted to update the same row twice" / ora-30926). deduplicate the source first: using (select distinct on (id) * from staging order by id, updated_at desc) as s :::

no in postgresql/oracle/sql server | filtering rows belongs in `where`, not `having` — putting it in `having` still works but forces the engine to aggregate rows it will then throw away. -- slow: aggregates everything, then discards select country, count(*) from orders group by country, status having status = 'paid'; -- fast: filters first, aggregates less, and can use an index on status select country, count(*) from orders where status = 'paid' group by country; the functional dependency rule standard sql requires every non-aggregated select-list column to appear in `group by` — unless it is *functionally dependent* on a grouped primary key. select c.id, c.email, c.full_name, count(o.id) as orders from customers c left join orders o on o.customer_id = c.id group by c.id; sql server, oracle and db2 require the expression to be repeated in full. bigquery, snowflake, duckdb and postgresql 16+ also accept `group by all`, which groups by every non-aggregated select-list column. filter — conditional aggregation select country, count(*) as all_orders, count(*) filter (where status = 'paid') as paid, count(*) filter (where status = 'refunded') as refunded, sum(total) filter (where created_at >= date '2026-01-01') as revenue_ytd from orders group by country; docs.h: order by & sorting deterministic sorting, null placement, collations, custom orderings and the cost of a sort. order by asc desc nulls first last collation custom sort case natural sort tie breaker stable without `order by` a result has **no defined order**. an unordered query that appears sorted is a coincidence of the current plan; adding an index, a parallel scan or more data changes it. select * from orders order by created_at desc, -- primary key of the sort id desc; -- tie-breaker makes the order deterministic ::: tip always add a unique tie-breaker sorting by a non-unique column leaves rows with equal keys in an arbitrary, unstable order. that silently breaks pagination: the same row can appear on page 1 and page 2. append the primary key. ::: null placement | engine | default for `asc` | `nulls first` / `nulls last` | | --- | --- | --- | | postgresql, oracle, db2 | nulls last | yes | | snowflake | nulls last | yes | | mysql, mariadb | nulls first | mariadb yes; mysql no | | sql server, synapse | nulls first | no | | sqlite | nulls first | 3.30+ yes | | bigquery, databricks, duckdb, clickhouse | nulls first | yes | order by case when due_date is null then 1 else 0 end, due_date; sorting by an expression, alias or position select total * 1.2 as gross from orders order by total * 1.2; -- expression select total * 1.2 as gross from orders order by gross; -- alias (works everywhere) select total * 1.2 as gross from orders order by 1; -- ordinal position ordinal positions are legal in every major engine but break the moment someone inserts a column into the select list. use them in ad-hoc analysis, not in stored code. custom orderings select * from tickets order by case priority when 'critical' then 1 when 'high' then 2 when 'normal' then 3 else 4 end, created_at; -- mysql / mariadb order by field(priority, 'critical', 'high', 'normal', 'low'); -- postgresql: an enum type sorts in declaration order automatically create type priority_t as enum ('critical','high','normal','low'); order by priority; -- uses the enum's natural order -- postgresql: array position order by array_position(array['critical','high','normal','low'], priority); collations collation decides how text compares and sorts: case sensitivity, accent sensitivity, and locale rules (in swedish 'ä' sorts after 'z'; in german it sorts with 'a'). select name from products order by name collate "de-de-x-icu"; select name from products order by name collate "c"; -- byte order: fastest, ascii-ish -- mysql order by name collate utf8mb4_de_0900_ai_ci; -- sql server order by name collate latin1_general_ci_ai; -- oracle alter session set nls_sort = 'german'; alter session set nls_comp = 'linguistic'; ::: warn changing a collation invalidates indexes a b-tree index stores keys in collation order. changing the collation of a column (or upgrading the os's icu/glibc version under postgresql) makes existing indexes silently wrong — lookups start missing rows. after a glibc or icu upgrade, `reindex` every text index. ::: natural sort `'item10'` sorts before `'item2'` in every text collation. real natural sort needs decomposition: select sku from products order by regexp_replace(sku, '[0-9]', '', 'g'), -- letter part coalesce(nullif(regexp_replace(sku, '[^0-9]', '', 'g'), ''), '0')::bigint; the cost of sorting a sort is o(n log n) and needs memory; when it exceeds the working-memory limit the engine spills to disk, often the single largest cost in a slow query. explain (analyze, buffers) select * from orders order by total desc; -- sort method: external merge disk: 24864kb ← spilled -- sort method: quicksort memory: 25kb ← fit in memory set work_mem = '64mb'; -- per sort node, per connection — raise carefully an index on the sort key can remove the sort entirely, if its direction matches: create index idx_orders_created_desc on orders (created_at desc, id desc); -- now this needs no sort node at all: select * from orders order by created_at desc, id desc limit 50;

docs.h: limit, offset & fetch row limiting in every dialect, why offset pagination degrades, and how keyset pagination fixes it. limit offset fetch first top rownum pagination keyset seek cursor row limiting ties percent every dialect, one operation select * from orders order by id limit 10 offset 20; -- postgresql, mysql, mariadb, sqlite, redshift, bigquery, snowflake, -- duckdb, clickhouse, cockroachdb, databricks, trino select * from orders order by id offset 20 rows fetch first 10 rows only; -- postgresql 8.4+, oracle 12c+, db2, sql server 2012+, mariadb 10.6+, snowflake select top 10 * from orders order by id; select top 10 percent * from orders order by total desc; select top 10 with ties * from orders order by total desc; -- includes ties on the 10th value select * from ( select o.*, rownum as rn from (select * from orders order by id) o where rownum <= 30 ) where rn > 20; -- rownum is assigned before order by, hence the double nesting. select * from orders order by id limit 20, 10; -- offset 20, limit 10 — easy to misread ::: warn limit without order by is meaningless "the first 10 rows" of an unordered set is whichever 10 the plan happened to produce. sql server and db2 reject `offset … fetch` without `order by` for exactly this reason; the other engines accept it and return non-deterministic results. ::: with ties include rows that tie with the last one, so a "top 10" can return 12 rows rather than cutting a tie arbitrarily. select * from orders order by total desc fetch first 10 rows with ties; postgresql=y~13+ sqlserver=y~top_n_with_ties oracle=y db2=y snowflake=n mysql=n sqlite=n bigquery=n redshift=n duckdb=y where it is missing, use `rank()`: select * from (select o.*, rank() over (order by total desc) as rnk from orders o) t where rnk <= 10; why offset pagination degrades `offset 100000` does not skip cheaply — the engine must generate, sort and discard 100,000 rows before returning the next 10. page 10,000 costs 1,000× page 1. offset 0 limit 20 → reads 20 rows ~1 ms offset 10000 limit 20 → reads 10,020 rows ~40 ms offset 500000 limit 20 → reads 500,020 rows ~2,000 ms there is a correctness problem too: if a row is inserted while a user pages, every subsequent page shifts by one — rows are seen twice or skipped entirely. keyset (seek) pagination remember the last row's sort key and ask for "the rows after it". constant time on every page, and stable under concurrent inserts. select id, created_at, total from orders order by created_at desc, id desc limit 20; select id, created_at, total from orders where (created_at, id) < (timestamp '2026-03-01 09:14:22', 918273) order by created_at desc, id desc limit 20; the matching index makes it a pure range scan: create index idx_orders_seek on orders (created_at desc, id desc); where created_at < @last_created or (created_at = @last_created and id < @last_id) | | offset | keyset | | --- | --- | --- | | deep page cost | linear in the offset | constant | | stable under concurrent writes | no | yes | | jump to page 8,347 | yes | no — only next/previous | | total page count | easy | needs a separate (expensive) count | ::: tip when you must show a page count don't run `count(*)` over the full table on every request. cache it, use an approximate count (`pg_class.reltuples`, `show table status`), or show "next page" affordances instead of numbered pages. most product surfaces do not need an exact total. :::

sql joins every join type with row-matching diagrams: inner, left, right, full, cross, self, lateral, semi and anti joins. join inner left right full outer cross self lateral apply semi anti natural using on join algorithms hash merge nested loop a join combines rows from two tables using a predicate. the join *type* decides what happens to rows with no match on the other side.
the sample data every example below runs against these two tables. note the deliberate mismatches: one employee has no department, one department has no employees. create table departments (id int primary key, name text); insert into departments values (1,'engineering'), (2,'finance'), (3,'legal'); create table employees (id int primary key, name text, dept_id int); insert into employees values (1,'ada', 1), (2,'grace', 1), (3,'linus', 2), (4,'margaret', null); -- no department select * from employees; inner join returns only rows with a match on **both** sides. unmatched rows from either table disappear. select e.name, d.name as department from employees e inner join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id; name | department -------+------------ ada | engineering grace | engineering linus | finance `join` alone means `inner join` in every engine. left join (left outer join) every row from the left table, plus matching right-hand columns — or `null` where there is no match. select e.name, d.name as department from employees e left join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id; name | department ---------+------------ ada | engineering grace | engineering linus | finance margaret | null ::: danger the left join that silently became an inner join putting a condition on the right-hand table in `where` filters out the `null`-extended rows, undoing the outer join: -- broken: behaves like an inner join select e.name, d.name from employees e left join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id where d.name <> 'legal'; -- null <> 'legal' is unknown → margaret dropped -- correct: filter in the on clause select e.name, d.name from employees e left join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id and d.name <> 'legal'; **rule:** conditions on the *outer* (optional) table belong in `on`. conditions on the *preserved* table belong in `where`. ::: right join the mirror image: every row from the right table. rarely written in practice — swapping the table order and using `left join` reads better and keeps the "preserved" table first. select e.name, d.name as department from employees e right join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id; name | department -------+------------ ada | engineering grace | engineering linus | finance null | legal postgresql=y mysql=y sqlite=y~3.39+ sqlserver=y oracle=y db2=y snowflake=y bigquery=y redshift=y duckdb=y clickhouse=y trino=y mariadb=y full outer join every row from both sides, matched where possible. select e.name, d.name as department from employees e full outer join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id; name | department ---------+------------ ada | engineering grace | engineering linus | finance margaret | null null | legal postgresql=y sqlserver=y oracle=y db2=y snowflake=y bigquery=y redshift=y duckdb=y trino=y sqlite=y~3.39+ mysql=n mariadb=n clickhouse=y select e.name, d.name as department from employees e left join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id union select e.name, d.name from employees e right join departments d on d.id = e.dept_id; -- union (not union all) removes the duplicated matched rows. cross join the cartesian product: every left row paired with every right row. `n × m` rows, no predicate. select e.name, d.name as department from employees e cross join departments d; legitimate uses: generating a dense calendar × dimension grid, building test data, or expanding a small lookup set. select d.day, p.id as product_id, coalesce(s.units, 0) as units from generate_series(date '2026-01-01', date '2026-01-31', interval '1 day') as d(day) cross join products p left join sales s on s.sold_on = d.day and s.product_id = p.id; ::: warn an accidental cross join is the classic runaway query omitting a join condition — or writing the old comma syntax and forgetting a `where` term — turns two million-row tables into 10¹² rows. if a query "hangs", check the plan for a nested loop with no join condition. ::: self join a table joined to itself, using aliases to distinguish the two roles. the standard way to walk a parent/child hierarchy one level. select e.name as employee, m.name as manager from employees e left join employees m on m.id = e.manager_id; select a.name, b.name, a.dept_id from employees a join employees b on b.dept_id = a.dept_id and b.id > a.id; for arbitrary-depth hierarchies you need a [recursive cte](/sql/cte/#with-recursive), not a self join. lateral join / cross apply a lateral subquery can reference columns from tables **earlier in the from clause** — effectively a correlated subquery that returns multiple rows and columns. the canonical use is "top n per group". select c.id, c.email, o.id as order_id, o.total, o.created_at from customers c cross join lateral ( select id, total, created_at from orders where customer_id = c.id -- references c — only legal because of lateral order by created_at desc limit 3 ) o; use `left join lateral … on true` to keep customers with no orders. select c.id, c.email, o.id, o.total from customers c cross apply (select top 3 id, total from orders where customer_id = c.id order by created_at desc) o; -- outer apply keeps customers with no orders (like left join lateral) postgresql=y~lateral oracle=y~both_spellings sqlserver=y~apply db2=y snowflake=y~lateral bigquery=w~unnest_correlation duckdb=y trino=y mysql=y~8.0.14+_lateral mariadb=n sqlite=n redshift=n~limited clickhouse=n cockroachdb=y semi and anti joins not spelled as join keywords in standard sql — expressed with `exists` / `not exists` and recognised by the optimizer. select c.* from customers c where exists (select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id); select c.* from customers c where not exists (select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id); a plain `inner join` would duplicate a customer once per order; the semi join returns each customer exactly once without a `distinct`. using and natural join select * fr

docs.d: Scalar, row, table and correlated subqueries; EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN, and when each produces a better plan.
docs.h: subqueries scalar, row, table and correlated subqueries; exists vs in vs join, and when each produces a better plan. subquery scalar correlated exists not exists in any all derived table inline view uncorrelated a subquery is a `select` nested inside another statement. four shapes, each legal in different positions: | shape | returns | legal in | | --- | --- | --- | | **scalar** | exactly one row, one column | `select` list, `where`, `set`, `having` | | **row** | one row, several columns | `where (a,b) = (select …)` | | **table** (derived table / inline view) | many rows and columns | `from`, `join` | | **correlated** | re-evaluated per outer row | anywhere, but conceptually a loop | scalar subqueries select o.id, o.total, o.total - (select avg(total) from orders) as diff_from_mean from orders o; ::: warn a scalar subquery returning more than one row is a runtime error "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression" (postgresql) / ora-01427 (oracle). it often only fires in production, when the data finally contains a duplicate. guard with `limit 1` plus a deterministic `order by`, or restructure as a join. ::: a scalar subquery that returns **zero** rows yields `null`, not an error — a quieter and often nastier bug. correlated subqueries a correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it is logically re-evaluated for every outer row. select e.name, e.salary, e.dept_id from employees e where e.salary > (select avg(e2.salary) from employees e2 where e2.dept_id = e.dept_id); the same result as a window function, which reads the table once instead of once per row: select name, salary, dept_id from ( select e.*, avg(salary) over (partition by dept_id) as dept_avg from employees e ) t where salary > dept_avg; ::: tip modern planners often decorrelate automatically postgresql, sql server, oracle and duckdb can rewrite many correlated subqueries into joins or hash aggregates. but "often" is not "always" — an `explain` showing a nested loop with a subplan executed millions of times means it did not, and you should rewrite by hand. ::: exists vs in vs join three ways to express "customers who have ordered": select c.* from customers c where exists (select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id); select c.* from customers c where c.id in (select customer_id from orders); select distinct c.* from customers c join orders o on o.customer_id = c.id; | | `exists` | `in` | `join` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | duplicates outer rows | no | no | yes — needs `distinct` | | safe when the inner set has nulls | yes | yes for `in`, **no** for `not in` | yes | | can select inner columns | no | no | yes | | typical plan | semi join | semi join (after unnesting) | hash/merge join + dedup | ::: danger not in with nulls returns nothing if the subquery yields even one `null`, `not in` can never be true. use `not exists`. full explanation in [null & three-valued logic](/sql/null/#the-not-in-trap). ::: `select 1` vs `select *` inside `exists` makes no difference — every engine discards the select list. write whichever you find clearer. any / all / some select * from products where price > all (select price from products where category = 'budget'); -- more than every one select * from products where price > any (select price from products where category = 'premium'); -- more than at least one `x = any (…)` is exactly `x in (…)`; `x <> all (…)` is exactly `x not in (…)` — including the `null` trap. `all` over an **empty** set is `true`; `any` over an empty set is `false`. postgresql=y mysql=y sqlserver=y oracle=y db2=y sqlite=n~in_only snowflake=y bigquery=n~use_in redshift=y duckdb=y derived tables a subquery in `from`. most engines require an alias. select country, avg(order_count) as avg_orders_per_customer from ( select c.id, c.country, count(o.id) as order_count from customers c left join orders o on o.customer_id = c.id group by c.id, c.country ) as per_customer -- alias required in postgresql, mysql, sql server group by country; beyond two levels of nesting, a [cte](/sql/cte/) reads far better and can be reused. subqueries in the select list select c.id, (select count(*) from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id) as order_count, (select max(total) from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id) as biggest_order from customers c; select c.id, coalesce(o.order_count, 0) as order_count, o.biggest_order from customers c left join ( select customer_id, count(*) as order_count, max(total) as biggest_order from orders group by customer_id ) o on o.customer_id = c.id; restrictions worth knowing **mysql** cannot modify a table and select from the same table in a subquery (`error 1093`). wrap the subquery in another derived table to force materialization. **sqlite** has no `all`/`any` quantifiers. **redshift** does not support correlated subqueries in every position — some forms raise "this type of correlated subquery pattern is not supported". **bigquery** requires correlated subqueries to be aggregated or `exists`-shaped; arbitrary correlation is limited.

docs.h: ctes & recursive queries with clauses for readability, with recursive for hierarchies and graphs, and the optimization-fence question. cte with clause common table expression recursive hierarchy tree graph materialized fence data modifying a **common table expression** names a subquery so the main query can reference it — sometimes several times — and so a pipeline reads top to bottom instead of inside out. with paid_orders as ( select * from orders where status = 'paid' ), customer_totals as ( select customer_id, count(*) as orders, sum(total) as revenue from paid_orders group by customer_id ), ranked as ( select ct.*, rank() over (order by revenue desc) as revenue_rank from customer_totals ct ) select c.email, r.orders, r.revenue, r.revenue_rank from ranked r join customers c on c.id = r.customer_id where r.revenue_rank <= 20 order by r.revenue_rank; postgresql=y mysql=y~8.0+ mariadb=y~10.2+ sqlite=y sqlserver=y oracle=y~9i+ db2=y snowflake=y bigquery=y redshift=y duckdb=y clickhouse=y trino=y databricks=y cockroachdb=y with recursive a recursive cte has two parts joined by `union all`: an **anchor** that produces the starting rows, and a **recursive term** that references the cte itself and runs repeatedly until it returns nothing. with recursive org as ( -- anchor: the root select id, name, manager_id, 1 as depth, cast(name as varchar(1000)) as path from employees where manager_id is null union all -- recursive term: one level down, per iteration select e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1, cast(o.path || ' > ' || e.name as varchar(1000)) from employees e join org o on o.id = e.manager_id where o.depth < 20 -- depth guard: stops runaway recursion ) select depth, path from org order by path; depth | path ------+-------------------------------- 1 | kathleen 2 | kathleen > ada 3 | kathleen > ada > grace 2 | kathleen > linus ::: note syntax note oracle, sql server and db2 do **not** use the `recursive` keyword — just `with`. postgresql, mysql, sqlite, mariadb, bigquery, snowflake and redshift require it. write `with recursive` where accepted; it is also documentation for the reader. ::: generating series with recursive days (d) as ( select date '2026-01-01' union all select d + interval '1 day' from days where d < date '2026-12-31' ) select d from days; engine shortcuts: `generate_series()` (postgresql, duckdb, cockroachdb), `generate_date_array()` (bigquery), `generator()` (snowflake), `numbers()` (clickhouse), `sequence()` (trino, databricks). graph traversal with cycle protection recursion over a graph loops forever unless you track visited nodes. with recursive reachable as ( select src, dst, array[src] as visited, 1 as hops from edges where src = 1 union all select e.src, e.dst, r.visited || e.dst, r.hops + 1 from edges e join reachable r on e.src = r.dst where not (e.dst = any (r.visited)) -- do not revisit and r.hops < 50 ) select distinct dst, min(hops) as shortest from reachable group by dst; postgresql 14+, db2 and oracle offer a declarative form: with recursive reachable (src, dst) as (…) cycle dst set is_cycle using path select * from reachable where not is_cycle; ::: danger an unbounded recursive cte will consume the machine without a depth guard or cycle check, a single cyclic edge produces infinite rows. mysql caps iterations at `cte_max_recursion_depth` (default 1000); sql server defaults to `option (maxrecursion 100)`. postgresql and sqlite have **no default limit** — add `where depth < n` yourself. ::: oracle's connect by oracle's proprietary hierarchical syntax predates recursive ctes and is still ubiquitous in oracle codebases: select level as depth, lpad(' ', 2*(level-1)) || name as tree, sys_connect_by_path(name, '>') as path from employees start with manager_id is null connect by prior id = manager_id order siblings by name; `level`, `sys_connect_by_path`, `connect_by_root`, `connect_by_isleaf` and `nocycle` come with it. oracle also supports the standard `with` form; new code should prefer it. data-modifying ctes postgresql lets `insert`/`update`/`delete … returning` appear inside a `with`, so a multi-table write becomes one atomic statement. with moved as ( delete from orders where created_at < now() - interval '2 years' returning * ) insert into orders_archive select * from moved; postgresql=y duckdb=y cockroachdb=y mariadb=n mysql=n sqlite=n sqlserver=n oracle=n snowflake=n bigquery=n redshift=n ::: warn all sub-statements see the same snapshot in a data-modifying cte every branch reads the database as it was at statement start. a `select` branch will **not** see rows written by an `insert` branch of the same statement. ::: is a cte an optimization fence? whether the engine inlines a cte into the main query or materializes it once changes plans dramatically. | engine | behaviour | | --- | --- | | postgresql ≤ 11 | always materialized — a hard optimization fence | | postgresql 12+ | inlined when referenced once and not recursive; `materialized` / `not materialized` force either way | | sql server, oracle | inlined by default; oracle has `/*+ materialize */` and `/*+ inline */` hints | | mysql 8 | materialized into a temporary table in most cases | | sqlite | inlined when possible (`materialized` hint available in 3.35+) | | bigquery, snowflake, redshift | generally inlined; a cte referenced n times may be **executed n times** | with expensive as materialized ( -- compute once, reuse select customer_id, sum(total) as revenue from orders group by customer_id ) select * from expensive a join expensive b on b.revenue = a.revenue and b.customer_id <> a.customer_id; ::: tip a cte referenced many times may be recomputed many times on warehouses that inline, a cte used in five places can run five times. if the cte is expensive, write it to a temporary table instead — and measure, because the opposite (an unnecessary materialization blocking predicate pushdown) is just as common. :::
