docs.h: sqlite a library, not a server. the most deployed database engine in the world — with type affinity and per-connection pragmas to understand. overview sqlite is not a client/server database. it is a c library that reads and writes an ordinary file, linked directly into your process. there is no daemon, no port, no configuration file and no user accounts — access control is filesystem permissions. it ships in every android and ios device, every major browser, python, and countless embedded systems, which makes it the most widely deployed database engine in existence. first release :: 2000 license :: public domain current :: 3.50.x deployment :: in-process library; one file per database concurrency :: many readers, one writer (wal mode) default isolation :: serializable best for :: embedded storage, application file formats, tests, edge/local-first apps, small-to-medium web apps ::: note sqlite competes with fopen(), not with postgresql the official framing is worth internalising. sqlite replaces bespoke file formats, not database servers. that said, a single-server web application with a read-heavy workload and wal enabled runs perfectly well on sqlite — the limit is concurrent *writers*, not data volume (the file limit is 281 tb). ::: architecture app.db the database: b-trees for every table and index app.db-wal write-ahead log (wal mode) app.db-shm shared-memory index for the wal every table is a b-tree keyed by `rowid` (an implicit 64-bit integer) unless declared `without rowid`, in which case it clusters on the declared primary key. `integer primary key` is special-cased as an alias for `rowid` — it costs nothing extra and is the cheapest key available. installation sudo apt install sqlite3 # cli; the library is almost certainly already present brew install sqlite python3 -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)" # already available everywhere cli sqlite3 app.db # opens or creates sqlite3 :memory: # in-memory sqlite3 -csv -header app.db "select * from t" > out.csv .tables .schema t .indexes t .mode box|csv|json|markdown .headers on .timer on .eqp on .import data.csv t .backup backup.db .dump .read script.sql .expert -- index suggestions .quit pragmas — the configuration surface pragma foreign_keys = on; -- off by default, and per connection pragma journal_mode = wal; -- persistent; readers no longer block the writer pragma synchronous = normal; -- safe under wal, much faster than full pragma busy_timeout = 5000; -- wait 5 s instead of failing with sqlite_busy pragma cache_size = -64000; -- 64 mb of page cache (negative = kib) pragma temp_store = memory; pragma optimize; -- run before closing a long-lived connection pragma integrity_check; ::: danger foreign_keys is off by default for backwards compatibility, sqlite parses foreign key declarations and does not enforce them unless `pragma foreign_keys = on` is executed on **each connection**. connection pools must set it in their per-connection initialisation, not once at startup. ::: type affinity sqlite is dynamically typed. declared column types are *affinities* — hints about preferred storage — not constraints. | declared type contains | affinity | stores | | --- | --- | --- | | `int` | integer | 1–8 byte signed integer | | `char`, `clob`, `text` | text | utf-8/16 string | | `blob` or nothing | blob | bytes, as-is | | `real`, `floa`, `doub` | real | 8-byte ieee float | | anything else | numeric | integer if it fits, else real, else text | create table t (age integer); insert into t values ('not a number'); -- accepted, stored as text create table t ( id integer primary key, age integer not null, name text not null ) strict; insert into t values (1, 'abc', 'x'); -- error: cannot store text value in integer column there are no native `date`, `time` or `boolean` types. store iso-8601 text (`'2026-08-13t09:15:00z'`) — it sorts and compares correctly — or a unix integer, and use `0`/`1` for booleans. what sqlite does not have | missing | workaround | | --- | --- | | `alter table` beyond add/drop/rename column | the [12-step table rebuild](/sql/alter/#sqlite-the-twelve-step-rebuild) | | stored procedures, triggers in a procedural language | application code (sql triggers do exist) | | `grant` / `revoke` / users | filesystem permissions | | `right`/`full outer join` before 3.39 | swap the tables, or use a union | | `any`/`all` quantifiers | `in` / `exists` | | materialized views | a real table plus a refresh routine | | concurrent writers | queue writes; wal allows concurrent *readers* | what it has that surprises people -- window functions (3.25+), ctes, returning (3.35+), upsert, json, generated columns insert into t (a) values (1) on conflict (a) do update set b = excluded.b returning *; -- full-text search with bm25 ranking create virtual table docs_fts using fts5(title, body); select *, bm25(docs_fts) as rank from docs_fts where docs_fts match 'sql and index' order by rank; -- query another database file in the same statement attach database 'archive.db' as arc; insert into arc.orders select * from main.orders where created_at < '2025-01-01'; performance ::: tip the single biggest speedup wrap inserts in an explicit transaction. each unwrapped `insert` is its own transaction with its own fsync — roughly 100/second on spinning media. batched inside one transaction, the same inserts run at tens of thousands per second. begin; insert into t values (…); -- ×10,000 commit; ::: pragma journal_mode = wal; -- concurrent readers, faster commits pragma synchronous = normal; -- safe with wal analyze; -- populate sqlite_stat1 so the planner has statistics explain query plan select …; -- readable plan output use prepared statements (they avoid reparsing), keep indexes on your filter and join columns, and remember that `select count(*)` is a full b-tree scan. backup sqlite3 app.db ".backup 'backup.db'" # safe online backup (uses the backup api) sqlite3 app.db ".dump" > app.sql # logical dump sqlite3 app.db "vacuum into 'compact.db'" # 3.27+: backup and compact in one step copying `app.db` with `cp` while a writer is active produces a corrupt file — the wal and shm contents are n

docs.h: sql server microsoft's flagship rdbms. t-sql, clustered indexes, columnstore, and a set of defaults that differ from every other engine. overview sql server is a mature enterprise rdbms with an unusually complete tooling story: a first-class procedural dialect (t-sql), an integrated columnstore engine for analytics, and deep diagnostic dmvs. it runs on windows, linux and containers, and azure sql database is the same engine as a managed service. first release :: 1989 license :: commercial (developer and express editions are free) current :: sql server 2025; azure sql database (evergreen) wire protocol :: tds, port 1433 default isolation :: read committed (lock-based, unless rcsi is enabled) best for :: enterprise oltp, .net stacks, htap with columnstore, bi workloads architecture a table is either a **heap** or a **clustered index** — and the clustered index *is* the table, exactly as in mysql/innodb. non-clustered indexes store the clustering key as their row locator, so a wide clustered key inflates every other index. `tempdb` is a shared scratch database used by sorts, hash spills, temp tables, and the row-version store when snapshot isolation is on. it is a frequent bottleneck; configure multiple equally-sized data files. installation & cli docker run -d --name mssql -e accept_eula=y -e mssql_sa_password='str0ng!pass' \ -p 1433:1433 mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest sqlcmd -s localhost,1433 -u sa -p 'str0ng!pass' -d master -c sqlcmd -s localhost -u sa -p '…' -i migrate.sql -b # -b: non-zero exit on error t-sql specifics select top 10 * from orders order by id; -- row limiting select * from orders order by id offset 20 rows fetch next 10 rows only; select isnull(bonus, 0), iif(total > 100, 'big', 'small'); select first_name + ' ' + last_name; -- + concatenates select * from c cross apply (select top 1 * from o where o.cid = c.id order by d desc) x; select * from [dbo].[order details]; -- bracket quoting go -- batch separator (client-side) set xact_abort on; begin try begin transaction; update accounts set balance = balance - @amt where id = @from; if @@rowcount = 0 throw 50001, 'account not found', 1; commit; end try begin catch if @@trancount > 0 rollback; throw; end catch indexes create clustered index ix_orders on dbo.orders (id); create nonclustered index ix_cust on dbo.orders (customer_id) include (total, status); create nonclustered index ix_open on dbo.orders (created_at) where status = 'open'; -- filtered create clustered columnstore index cci_facts on dbo.fact_sales; -- analytics, 10x compression create index ix_a on dbo.t (a) with (online = on, data_compression = page); concurrency ::: danger the default makes readers block writers lock-based `read committed` means a reporting query can block an `update` and vice versa. enabling row versioning usually removes an entire class of timeouts: alter database app set read_committed_snapshot on with rollback immediate; the cost is tempdb space for the version store. almost every modern deployment turns it on. ::: ::: warn triggers fire once per statement `inserted` and `deleted` are **tables** containing every affected row. a trigger written as `select @id = id from inserted` silently processes one arbitrary row of a multi-row update. ::: diagnostics set statistics io, time on; select top 20 qs.execution_count, qs.total_worker_time/1000 as cpu_ms, qs.total_elapsed_time/qs.execution_count/1000 as avg_ms, substring(st.text, (qs.statement_start_offset/2)+1, 200) as stmt from sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs cross apply sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) st order by qs.total_worker_time desc; select * from sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats where database_id = db_id(); select * from sys.dm_os_wait_stats order by wait_time_ms desc; select * from sys.dm_tran_locks; backup & ha backup database app to disk='d:\bk\full.bak' with compression, checksum; backup log app to disk='d:\bk\log.trn'; restore database app from disk='d:\bk\full.bak' with norecovery; restore log app from disk='d:\bk\log.trn' with stopat='2026-08-13t09:15:00', recovery; always on availability groups provide synchronous or asynchronous replicas with automatic failover and readable secondaries. best practices enable `read_committed_snapshot` unless you have a specific reason not to. keep the clustered key narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing. treat `sys.dm_db_missing_index_details` as a hint, not a script — it suggests wide, overlapping indexes. use `sp_executesql` with parameters, never string concatenation, for dynamic sql. configure multiple tempdb data files sized equally. remember: `unique` permits only **one** null here, and `datediff` counts boundary crossings, not elapsed time.

docs.h: oracle database the enterprise incumbent. pl/sql, rac, deep partitioning, and a dialect with more surprises than any other. overview oracle database is the enterprise standard in banking, telecoms and erp. its differentiators are pl/sql (a full procedural language with packages), real application clusters (active-active shared-storage clustering), a very sophisticated optimizer, and flashback (query and restore the past without a backup). first release :: 1979 license :: commercial; express edition (xe) is free with limits current :: 23ai default port :: 1521 default isolation :: read committed (no repeatable read — only read committed and serializable) best for :: large enterprise oltp and dw, workloads needing rac or data guard oracle-isms that catch everyone ::: danger the empty string is null oracle stores `''` as `null` in `varchar2`. `where name = ''` never matches anything, and `not null` columns reject empty strings. no other major engine behaves this way, and it breaks naive migrations in both directions. ::: | oracle | everywhere else | | --- | --- | | `select … from dual` | `select` with no `from` | | `minus` | `except` | | `nvl(a,b)`, `nvl2`, `decode` | `coalesce`, `case` | | `varchar2` | `varchar` | | `number` | `integer` / `numeric` | | `date` includes a time | `date` is date-only | | `sysdate`, `systimestamp` | `current_timestamp` | | no `on update` on foreign keys | `on update cascade` | | identifiers fold to uppercase | postgresql folds to lowercase | | `rownum` assigned before `order by` | — | row limiting select * from orders order by id fetch first 10 rows only; select * from orders order by total desc fetch first 10 rows with ties; -- 11g and earlier: rownum is assigned before order by, so it must be nested select * from (select * from orders order by id) where rownum <= 10; hierarchical queries select level, lpad(' ', 2*(level-1)) || name as tree, sys_connect_by_path(name, '/') as path, connect_by_isleaf as is_leaf from employees start with manager_id is null connect by nocycle prior id = manager_id order siblings by name; oracle also supports standard `with` recursive ctes; prefer them in new code. pl/sql create or replace package body orders_pkg as function lifetime_value(p_customer_id number) return number is v_total number; begin select nvl(sum(total), 0) into v_total from orders where customer_id = p_customer_id; return v_total; exception when no_data_found then return 0; end; end orders_pkg; / the trailing `/` is required to execute a pl/sql block in sql*plus — scripts fail silently without it. partitioning & performance create table sales (id number, sold_on date, amount number(12,2)) partition by range (sold_on) interval (numtoyminterval(1,'month')) (partition p0 values less than (date '2024-01-01')); explain plan for select …; select * from table(dbms_xplan.display); select * from table(dbms_xplan.display_cursor(format => 'allstats last')); -- actual exec dbms_stats.gather_table_stats('app', 'orders'); flashback select * from employees as of timestamp (systimestamp - interval '1' hour); select * from employees versions between timestamp … and …; flashback table employees to before drop; -- undrop from the recycle bin flashback table employees to timestamp …; best practices prefer standard sql (`coalesce`, `case`, `fetch first`, `with`) over the oracle-only spellings in new code. use bind variables everywhere — literal-laden sql floods the shared pool with unshareable cursors. never update primary keys; there is no `on update cascade`. handle the `'' is null` behaviour explicitly in any cross-engine code. gather statistics after bulk loads; oracle's optimizer is heavily statistics-driven. watch for `ora-01555 snapshot too old` — undo retention too small for your long queries.

docs.h: amazon redshift aws mpp warehouse forked from postgresql 8.0. distribution keys and sort keys are the whole performance story. overview redshift is a massively parallel columnar warehouse. it speaks the postgresql wire protocol (so `psql` and postgresql drivers work) but the engine underneath is entirely different: columnar storage, mpp execution across slices, and no indexes at all. launched :: 2013 base :: forked from postgresql 8.0 — expect no modern pg features deployment :: provisioned (ra3) or serverless protocol :: postgresql, port 5439 best for :: batch analytics on aws, star-schema warehouses, s3 lakehouse queries via spectrum architecture leader node parses sql, builds the plan, distributes code to compute nodes └── compute node ×n └── slices each slice owns a portion of every table's data rows are distributed across slices by the **distribution style**, and within each slice they are stored in 1 mb column blocks with **zone maps** (min/max per block) that let the scanner skip blocks. there are no indexes — the sort key is what makes pruning possible. distribution and sort keys create table fact_orders ( order_id bigint, customer_id bigint, order_date date, total numeric(12,2) ) diststyle key distkey (customer_id) -- co-locate joins on customer_id compound sortkey (order_date); -- zone-map pruning on date ranges | style | behaviour | use when | | --- | --- | --- | | `auto` | redshift decides and may change it | the default; fine to start with | | `key` | rows with equal key land on the same slice | large fact tables joined on that key | | `all` | full copy on every node | small dimension tables (< a few million rows) | | `even` | round-robin | no natural join key | ::: danger ds_bcast_inner in a plan means a table is being broadcast every compute node receives a full copy of the inner table across the network — usually the single largest cost in a slow redshift query. fix it by giving both tables the same `distkey`, or by making the small side `diststyle all`. ::: loading copy fact_orders from 's3://bucket/orders/' iam_role 'arn:aws:iam::123:role/redshiftcopy' format as parquet; unload ('select * from fact_orders where order_date >= ''2026-01-01''') to 's3://bucket/export/' iam_role '…' parquet parallel on; split source files into a multiple of the slice count so every slice loads in parallel. row-by-row `insert` is orders of magnitude slower and should never be used for bulk data. maintenance & monitoring select * from svv_table_info order by size desc; -- skew, unsorted %, size select * from stl_alert_event_log order by event_time desc limit 20; -- start here select * from svl_query_summary where query = 12345; vacuum full fact_orders; -- restore sort order after big loads analyze fact_orders; best practices set a `distkey` on the join column of your largest fact table; use `diststyle all` for small dimensions. put the column you filter by date on the `sortkey`. watch for skew in `svv_table_info` — one overloaded slice makes the whole cluster wait. `analyze` and `vacuum` after large loads. remember constraints are **not enforced** — the optimizer trusts them, so violating them can produce wrong results. use spectrum external tables for cold data in s3 rather than loading everything.

docs.h: snowflake storage separated from compute. virtual warehouses, zero-copy cloning, time travel — and a cost model you must actively manage. overview snowflake separates storage (columnar micro-partitions in cloud object storage) from compute (virtual warehouses you size and suspend independently). multiple warehouses read the same data with no contention, which is what makes concurrent workloads straightforward. launched :: 2014 deployment :: managed saas on aws, azure and gcp compute :: virtual warehouses, xs → 6xl, resized instantly storage :: immutable micro-partitions (~16 mb compressed) with automatic metadata best for :: cloud data warehousing, data sharing, semi-structured data at scale compute & cost create warehouse analytics with warehouse_size = 'medium' auto_suspend = 60 -- seconds of idle before suspending — the biggest single saving auto_resume = true min_cluster_count = 1 max_cluster_count = 4; -- multi-cluster serves concurrency, not speed alter warehouse analytics set warehouse_size = 'large'; -- instant, no data movement ::: tip sizing up vs scaling out a **larger** warehouse makes a single query faster (more nodes on one job). **more clusters** let more queries run at once. choosing the wrong axis is the most common snowflake cost mistake. ::: semi-structured data create table events (raw variant); copy into events from @stage file_format = (type = json); select raw:user.name::string as name, raw:items[0].sku::string as first_sku, f.value:qty::number as qty from events, lateral flatten(input => raw:items) f; time travel & cloning select * from orders at (offset => -3600); -- one hour ago select * from orders before (statement => '01a2b3c4-…'); -- before a bad statement undrop table orders; create table orders_test clone orders; -- zero-copy: instant, no extra storage create database dev clone prod; -- an entire environment in seconds pipelines create stream orders_stream on table orders; -- change data capture create task load_summary warehouse = etl schedule = '5 minute' when system$stream_has_data('orders_stream') as merge into summary using orders_stream …; create pipe p auto_ingest = true as copy into t from @stage; -- snowpipe performance & governance select * from snowflake.account_usage.query_history order by total_elapsed_time desc limit 20; select * from snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_metering_history; alter table big_table cluster by (event_date); -- only worth it on very large tables alter table t add search optimization; -- point lookups; extra cost snowflake enforces strict rbac — privileges are granted only to roles, and roles are hierarchical. best practices set `auto_suspend` to 60 seconds on every warehouse. separate warehouses per workload (etl / bi / ad-hoc) so one cannot starve another. use `grant … on future` so new objects inherit access. only `not null` is enforced — every other constraint is metadata for the optimizer. clone rather than copy for dev/test environments. query the result cache deliberately: byte-identical sql on unchanged data is free.

docs.h: google bigquery serverless columnar warehouse. no indexes, no servers — partitioning, clustering and bytes scanned are the whole model. overview bigquery has no instances to size. you submit sql; google allocates slots and runs it against columnar storage. pricing is per **bytes scanned** (on-demand) or per reserved slot capacity, which makes query shape a direct financial concern. launched :: 2011 (googlesql dialect since 2016) deployment :: fully serverless on google cloud namespace :: project → dataset → table pricing :: bytes scanned (on-demand) or slot reservations best for :: very large analytical workloads, event data, ml in sql (bqml) cost control comes first ::: danger limit does not reduce cost the scan has already happened by the time `limit` applies. what actually reduces bytes scanned: **name your columns.** columnar storage means `select *` on a 200-column table can cost 50× the query you needed. **filter on the partition column** so whole partitions are pruned. **dry-run first**: `bq query --dry_run` reports the bytes before you pay for them. **cached results are free** — for byte-identical query text on unchanged data, for 24 hours. ::: create table analytics.events ( event_time timestamp, user_id string, name string, params array<struct<key string, value string>> ) partition by date(event_time) cluster by user_id, name options (partition_expiration_days = 400, require_partition_filter = true); -- rejects queries that would scan everything googlesql specifics select * except (password_hash) from users; select * replace (lower(email) as email) from users; select safe_cast(raw as int64), safe.parse_date('%y-%m-%d', raw); -- null instead of error select * from orders qualify row_number() over (partition by cid order by t desc) = 1; select e.event_id, p.key, p.value from events e, unnest(e.params) as p; -- flatten repeated nested `array<struct<…>>` columns are the idiomatic bigquery model: they store one-to-many relationships inside the row, so `unnest` costs nothing compared to a shuffle-inducing join. loading & streaming load data into analytics.events from files (format = 'parquet', uris = ['gs://bucket/events/*.parquet']); docs.h: mariadb the community fork of mysql. compatible where it matters, with sequences, system-versioned tables and extra storage engines. overview mariadb was forked from mysql in 2009 by its original authors after the oracle acquisition. it remains largely drop-in compatible for applications, but the two have diverged: they are no longer wire- or feature-identical, and replication between them is not supported in both directions. first release :: 2009 license :: gplv2 — fully open source current :: 11.8 lts default port :: 3306 best for :: mysql workloads wanting an open-source guarantee, plus galera clustering what mariadb has that mysql does not create sequence order_seq start with 1000 increment by 1; -- real sequences select nextval(order_seq); create table employees (id int primary key, salary decimal(12,2)) with system versioning; -- temporal tables select * from employees for system_time as of timestamp '2026-01-01 00:00:00'; insert into t (a) values (1) returning id; -- returning on insert/delete select * from t order by x nulls last; -- nulls first/last additional storage engines ship in the box: **aria** (crash-safe myisam successor), **columnstore** (columnar analytics), **spider** (sharding), **connect** (federated external data). where it differs from mysql | | mysql 8 | mariadb 11 | | --- | --- | --- | | json type | native binary | alias for longtext + a validity check | | sequences | no | yes | | temporal tables | no | yes | | `returning` | no | yes | | invisible columns | no | yes | | clustering | group replication / innodb cluster | galera (synchronous multi-master) | | data dictionary | transactional | file-based | | optimizer | cost model overhaul in 8.0 | independent lineage | ::: warn migration is not symmetric moving mysql → mariadb is usually straightforward. moving mariadb → mysql, or replicating between them, is not supported and breaks on json handling, sequences and system-versioned tables. ::: galera clustering every node holds a full copy; writes are certified across the cluster before commit. + no replica lag, any node accepts writes, automatic node rejoin − write throughput is bounded by the slowest node; hotspot rows cause certification conflicts − requires innodb, primary keys on every table, and a quorum (3+ nodes) best practices treat it as its own database, not "mysql with a different name", once you use its unique features. use `utf8mb4` and check `sql_mode` exactly as with mysql. galera needs a primary key on every table — a table without one will not replicate correctly. everything on the [mysql page](/databases/mysql/) about innodb, indexes and `sql_mode` applies here too.

docs.h: clickhouse extremely fast columnar analytics. mergetree engines, sparse primary indexes and a deliberately non-standard write model. overview clickhouse is an open-source columnar olap database designed for very high ingest rates and sub-second aggregation over billions of rows. it achieves that partly by giving up things oltp users expect: there are no real transactions, updates are asynchronous, and uniqueness is not enforced. first release :: 2016 (yandex) license :: apache 2.0 default ports :: 9000 (native), 8123 (http) best for :: observability, event analytics, time series, real-time dashboards not for :: oltp, frequent single-row updates, workloads needing transactions mergetree the table engine is mandatory and determines everything. create table events ( event_time datetime, user_id uint64, name lowcardinality(string), duration uint32 ) engine = mergetree order by (user_id, event_time) -- also the sparse primary index partition by toyyyymm(event_time) ttl event_time + interval 90 day; -- automatic expiry the `order by` clause is the sorting key **and** the sparse primary index: one index entry per ~8192 rows. queries that filter on a prefix of it skip whole granules. queries that do not are full scans — which clickhouse is still remarkably fast at, but the difference is orders of magnitude. | engine | behaviour | | --- | --- | | `mergetree` | the base: sorted, partitioned, background-merged parts | | `replacingmergetree(ver)` | deduplicates by sorting key during merges — *eventually* | | `summingmergetree` | pre-aggregates numeric columns on merge | | `aggregatingmergetree` | stores aggregate function states | | `replicatedmergetree` | adds replication via clickhouse keeper | ::: danger deduplication is eventual, not immediate `replacingmergetree` removes duplicates when background merges happen — which may be minutes or hours later, or never for parts in different partitions. queries must use `final` (expensive) or aggregate explicitly (`argmax`) if they need deduplicated results *now*. ::: writes alter table events update duration = 0 where user_id = 42; -- a "mutation": async, rewrites parts alter table events delete where event_time < '2025-01-01'; -- same delete from events where user_id = 42; -- lightweight delete (23.3+), marks rows select * from system.mutations where is_done = 0; -- track progress insert in **large batches** (tens of thousands of rows). many small inserts create many small parts and overwhelm the background merge scheduler — the classic "too many parts" error. dialect select tostartofmonth(event_time) as m, count(), uniqexact(user_id), quantile(0.95)(duration) from events where event_time >= now() - interval 30 day group by m order by m; select * from events order by user_id, event_time desc limit 1 by user_id; -- latest per user select countif(status = 'error'), sumif(duration, status = 'ok') from events; -- -if combinators select name, arrayjoin(tags) as tag from articles; materialized views are insert triggers create materialized view daily_mv engine = summingmergetree order by day as select todate(event_time) as day, count() as events from events group by day; it fires on `insert` into the source table only. it does **not** see pre-existing rows and does not react to deletes. best practices choose `order by` to match your most common filter prefix — it is the single most important decision. use `lowcardinality(string)` for columns with a small distinct set; it is a large compression and speed win. batch inserts; never insert row by row. prefer append-only modelling over updates. use `uniqexact` only when you need exactness — `uniq` (hll) is far cheaper. monitor `system.parts`, `system.mutations` and `system.query_log`.

docs.h: trino / presto a sql engine with no storage of its own. federates queries across hive, iceberg, postgresql, kafka and dozens more. overview trino (formerly prestosql, forked from facebook's presto) is a distributed query engine that stores nothing. connectors expose external systems as catalogs, and one query can join across them — object storage, a relational database and a message queue in a single statement. origin :: presto at facebook (2012); trino fork 2020 license :: apache 2.0 default port :: 8080 architecture :: coordinator + workers, in-memory pipelined execution best for :: data lake and lakehouse querying, federation, interactive analytics over iceberg/delta catalog.schema.table └── catalog = a configured connector instance (hive, iceberg, postgresql, kafka…) select o.id, o.total, c.email from iceberg.warehouse.orders o join postgresql.public.customers c on c.id = o.customer_id where o.order_date >= date '2026-01-01'; dialect trino follows ansi sql closely and is the reference implementation many "modern sql" features are learned from. select approx_distinct(user_id), approx_percentile(duration, 0.95) from events; select id, t.tag from articles cross join unnest(tags) as t(tag); select try(cast(raw as integer)) from staging; -- null instead of failing select date_trunc('month', ts) as m, count(*) from events group by 1; select filter(scores, x -> x > 5), transform(scores, x -> x * 2) from t; -- lambdas table maintenance (iceberg) alter table iceberg.warehouse.orders execute optimize; -- compact small files alter table iceberg.warehouse.orders execute expire_snapshots(retention_threshold => '7d'); select * from iceberg.warehouse."orders$snapshots"; -- metadata tables select * from iceberg.warehouse.orders for version as of 1234567; -- time travel performance trino is **in-memory and pipelined** — there is no spill-to-disk checkpointing like spark, so a query that exceeds cluster memory fails rather than degrading. that is a deliberate trade for interactive latency. push filters down to the connector; check with `explain (type distributed)`. partition and sort the underlying files — trino's speed depends on skipping them. avoid `order by` on very large results; the final sort happens on one node. small files are the number-one lakehouse performance problem; compact regularly. best practices use it as a query layer, not a storage layer — durability belongs to the connectors. set per-query memory limits so one analyst cannot take out the cluster. prefer iceberg or delta over raw hive tables for reliable schema evolution and snapshot isolation. federation is powerful and easy to misuse: joining a billion-row lake table to a live oltp database will hammer the oltp database.

docs.h: databricks sql ansi-mode spark sql over delta lake, with unity catalog governance and photon vectorized execution. overview databricks sql is the warehouse-style interface to the databricks lakehouse: spark sql (in ansi mode) executing over **delta lake** tables in object storage, accelerated by the photon engine and governed by unity catalog. founded :: 2013 (creators of apache spark) storage :: delta lake — parquet + a transaction log namespace :: catalog.schema.table (unity catalog) best for :: lakehouse architectures, etl + bi + ml on one copy of the data delta lake delta adds a transaction log over parquet, which buys acid transactions, schema enforcement, time travel and efficient upserts on object storage. create table main.sales.orders (id bigint, total decimal(12,2), order_date date) using delta partitioned by (order_date); merge into orders t using staging s on t.id = s.id when matched then update set * when not matched then insert *; select * from orders version as of 42; select * from orders timestamp as of '2026-08-01'; describe history orders; optimize orders zorder by (customer_id); -- compact files + colocate related data vacuum orders retain 168 hours; -- remove files older than the retention window dialect set ansi_mode = true; -- errors on overflow and invalid casts instead of returning null select explode(items) as item from orders; select * from orders qualify row_number() over (partition by cid order by d desc) = 1; select collect_list(sku), collect_set(sku) from order_items group by order_id; select try_cast(raw as int), try_divide(a, b) from staging; select * from read_files('s3://bucket/events/', format => 'parquet'); ::: warn legacy spark sql silently returns null without ansi mode, an invalid cast or an arithmetic overflow yields `null` rather than an error — bad data propagates quietly through a pipeline. enable ansi mode on new workloads. ::: governance & pipelines unity catalog provides a three-level namespace with table-, row- and column-level access control, lineage and audit across workspaces. delta live tables declares pipelines as sql with built-in expectations: create or refresh streaming table clean_orders ( constraint valid_total expect (total > 0) on violation drop row ) as select * from stream(main.raw.orders); best practices run `optimize` with `zorder` on the columns you filter by; small files are the main performance problem. set a sensible `vacuum` retention — too short breaks time travel and concurrent readers. partition on low-cardinality columns only; over-partitioning creates the small-file problem it was meant to solve. use liquid clustering instead of static partitioning for evolving access patterns. enable ansi mode so type errors surface immediately.

docs.d: Horizontally scalable, geo-partitioned SQL with the PostgreSQL wire protocol and serializable isolation by default.
docs.h: cockroachdb horizontally scalable, geo-partitioned sql with the postgresql wire protocol and serializable isolation by default. overview cockroachdb is a distributed sql database: data is split into ranges, replicated with raft, and rebalanced automatically across nodes. it speaks the postgresql wire protocol, so most postgresql drivers and tools work unchanged — but the execution model is distributed, and that changes how you design schemas. first release :: 2015 license :: cockroachdb software license (source-available); free tier available protocol :: postgresql, port 26257 default isolation :: serializable — the only mainstream database that defaults to it best for :: multi-region oltp, systems needing survivability and strong consistency distribution model table → ranges (~512 mb each) → 3+ replicas via raft consensus leaseholder serves reads for its range; writes need a quorum. ::: danger sequential primary keys create a hotspot every insert with a monotonically increasing key targets the same range, so one node does all the work — the opposite of what you deployed a distributed database for. use `uuid` (with `gen_random_uuid()`), `unique_rowid()`, or hash-sharded indexes: create table events (id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(), ts timestamptz); create index on events (ts) using hash with (bucket_count = 8); ::: multi-region alter database app set primary region 'eu-west-1'; alter database app add region 'us-east-1'; alter table users set locality regional by row; -- each row lives near its user alter table countries set locality global; -- fast reads everywhere, slower writes this is the feature that distinguishes cockroachdb: data residency and read latency become declarative properties of the table. serializable by default because the default isolation is `serializable`, transactions can be aborted with a retry error (sqlstate `40001`) when they conflict. **applications must implement retry** — this is not optional. begin; savepoint cockroach_restart; -- work release savepoint cockroach_restart; commit; -- on error 40001: rollback to savepoint cockroach_restart and retry with backoff differences from postgresql | | postgresql | cockroachdb | | --- | --- | --- | | isolation default | read committed | serializable | | retry required | no | yes | | extensions (postgis, etc.) | yes | spatial built in; no arbitrary extensions | | triggers / stored procedures | full | limited | | `select for update` | yes | yes | | foreign keys | yes | yes, but cross-range checks cost network round trips | best practices avoid sequential primary keys; use uuids or hash-sharded indexes. keep transactions short — distributed contention is far more expensive than single-node contention. implement retry logic before you go to production, not after the first `40001`. use `regional by row` for user data and `global` for small reference tables. batch writes; each statement may involve consensus across regions.

-- returning merge into t using (values (1, 'a')) as s (id, name) on t.id = s.id when matched then update set name = s.name when not matched then insert (id, name) values (s.id, s.name); blu acceleration db2 luw can store tables **column-organized** with in-memory vectorized processing and actionable compression — analytics performance inside the same engine serving oltp. create table fact_sales (…) organize by column; administration db2 connect to sample user db2inst1 using password db2 "select tabname from syscat.tables where tabschema = current schema" db2 "runstats on table app.orders with distribution and detailed indexes all" db2 backup database sample to /backup compress db2look -d sample -e -o schema.sql # extract ddl db2move sample export # data movement select * from syscat.tables where tabschema = current schema; docs.h: azure synapse mpp t-sql warehousing on azure. distribution strategy replaces single-node index tuning. overview azure synapse analytics provides two very different sql experiences: **dedicated sql pools** (a provisioned mpp warehouse, formerly azure sql data warehouse) and **serverless sql pools** (pay-per-query t-sql over files in a data lake). microsoft fabric warehouse is the successor product and shares much of the engine. dialect :: t-sql (a subset — not everything from sql server is available) dedicated pool :: provisioned mpp, billed by dwu, 60 distributions serverless pool :: query parquet/csv/delta in adls, billed per tb scanned best for :: azure-native warehousing, existing t-sql and microsoft bi estates distribution is the whole design a dedicated pool always has **60 distributions**. how rows map to them determines whether a join needs a data movement step. create table fact_sales (…) with (distribution = hash(customer_id), -- co-locate joins on this column clustered columnstore index, partition (order_date range right for values ('2026-01-01','2026-02-01'))); create table dim_country (…) with (distribution = replicate); -- small dimensions create table staging_raw (…) with (distribution = round_robin, heap); -- landing tables | strategy | use for | | --- | --- | | `hash(col)` | large fact tables; pick the most common join key | | `replicate` | dimensions under ~2 gb — a copy on every node removes movement | | `round_robin` | staging and load tables with no natural key | ::: danger data movement is the cost when two joined tables are distributed on different columns, synapse must shuffle or broadcast — visible as `shuffle_move` or `broadcast_move` in the plan. aligning the hash column of the tables you join is the single highest-impact tuning action. ::: loading & querying files copy into fact_sales from 'https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/data/sales/*.parquet' with (file_type = 'parquet', credential = (identity = 'managed identity')); -- serverless pool, no ingestion at all: select top 100 * from openrowset( bulk 'https://acct.dfs.core.windows.net/data/sales/*.parquet', format = 'parquet') as r; diagnostics select * from sys.dm_pdw_exec_requests order by total_elapsed_time desc; select * from sys.dm_pdw_request_steps where request_id = 'qid12345'; -- look for *_move steps select * from sys.dm_pdw_nodes_db_partition_stats; -- skew per distribution create statistics st_customer on fact_sales (customer_id); -- must be created manually best practices create statistics explicitly — unlike sql server, synapse does not always create them automatically, and the mpp optimizer is helpless without them. use clustered columnstore for large tables; heaps only for staging. avoid `hash` distribution on a column with heavy skew — one distribution ends up doing all the work. pause dedicated pools when idle; they bill while provisioned. serverless pools charge per tb scanned, so partitioned parquet and column pruning matter exactly as in bigquery. not all t-sql is supported: no cross-database queries, limited triggers, no `merge` in older versions.
